content: This site seems remarkably impressive; it really shows the potential for autoformalization.
https://beta.prove2.me/

From the paper:

The closet community effort is Tau Ceti, which aims to build an AI-authored foundation-layer library downstream of Mathlib, but explicitly disavows frontier results such as recent research papers and requires every roadmap to make contact with material already in Mathlib or Tau Ceti. Prove2Me is orthogonal: it focuses on the application layer and lets a researcher launch a mission for their own paper or textbook regardless of its distance from existing libraries.

There's apparently no mention of lean-pool or LeanEval.

There are some nice ideas, but it's not enforcing common Lean/Mathlib version, which will impact reusability.

Finally, Prove2Me supports multiple verification environments, each pinned to a specific Mathlib and toolchain version, and the submitting agent selects the target environment. A theorem is accepted once it compiles in the corresponding backend. Environments are fully isolated from one another, so that a result always carries the exact context needed to reproduce it.

Formalpedia builds on curated foundational libraries such as Mathlib, CSLib, and PhysLib rather than competing with them: it focuses on the application layer, where results are one-off and mutually independent. We also hope that some of what accumulates on the platform will eventually be contributed back to these libraries. Formalpedia also shares the open spirit of registries of Lean-verified results such as Palomar and TheoremDB, but goes further in two ways: every statement is individually importable, so it can be reused easily in someone else’s proof; and an accompanying harness opens the work of formalization itself to a broader community.

Prove2Me also provides a search API over the corpus. The harness requires every agent to submit a detailed, standardized natural-language description alongside its Lean statement (Section 3.1), which is what the search API indexes. Agents are also instructed to search before they submit: reuse an existing theorem where one exists, and introduce a new statement only when none does.

Finally, reuse is also rewarded on Prove2Me. A contributor earns credit not only for closing an open theorem, but for proposing a statement that other proofs later import, which is this platform’s form of citation. The incentive thus points the same way as the mechanism: a theorem is worth more the more often it is built upon.

Here is a sample proof sketch which relies on 3 (possibly unproven) lemmas (given in the first 3 import lines):

import Theorems.Thm_mme_omega_eq_strassen
import Theorems.Thm_mme_tensorRank_le_strassenRank
import Theorems.Thm_mme_strassenRank_le_tensorRank

open MME

universe u

/-! # Sketch: `matMulExp = matMulExp_strassen`

Decomposition of child A into the two halves of the rank-witness correspondence:

  * `mme_tensorRank_le_strassenRank` — restriction witness ⇒ decomposition witness;
  * `mme_strassenRank_le_tensorRank` — decomposition witness ⇒ restriction witness.

The sketch assembles them: antisymmetry of the two inequalities gives
`tensorRank T = strassenRank T` for every tensor `T`, and rewriting that pointwise
under the shared `iInf` collapses the two exponents to a single value. -/

theorem solution {K : Type u} [Field K] :
    matMulExp K = matMulExp_strassen K := by
  have hrank : ∀ {d : ℕ} {V : Fin d → Type u} [∀ i, AddCommGroup (V i)]
      [∀ i, Module K (V i)] (T : PiTensorProduct K V), tensorRank T = strassenRank T :=
    fun T => le_antisymm (mme_tensorRank_le_strassenRank T) (mme_strassenRank_le_tensorRank T)
  simp only [matMulExp, matMulExp_strassen, hrank]

A bit of confusing terminology introduced by me: if you're not using module, you're not using the module system :) . So one of the things that I found was a source of friction using Prove2Me is the requirement that you human-verify the mathematics that you're submitting in a Mission before a campaign can be published.

I'm a big fan of having a human verification step for whether you've got the right definitions, but I think it's at the wrong place in the lifecycle for the current phase of AI development. It took like 15 minutes of clicking to (ignoring the instructions) approve the 30 theorems that I wanted to formalize, which was probably 20% of the total human time I spent managing the 3-account experiment detailed #FLT > Anthropic Vinogradov experiment . I had to re-click some of them because the Lean statements contained compile errors that needed to be fixed, and it only tries to compile after the human approval step. (I am not fluent in Lean, and the math I was formalizing I've not thought about in 20 years, so I'm not qualified to check them anyway.)

I think those design decisions were probably good when made but are a bit stale now. Like, a year ago, agent formalization was really expensive, and it made sense to spend attention on approving the campaign matched the math you wanted before spending the tokens.

But now, especially if we want to have a goal of formalizing a great deal of textbook and graduate mathematics, one kinda wants to be able to just point your agent at what your goal is, and potentially have the human approval be after you've confirmed you've got a Lean formalization and want to make sure it's doing the cleanest/preferred definitions of what you wanted to formalize.

Like I would love to see several people pick textbook math projects of a somewhat more ambitious scope than Vinogradov's theorem, and upload those campaigns to Prove2Me, and we can run a 20-person crowd experiment on doing autoformalization on Prove2Me, and then try to use the data to optimize the collaboration.

The platform worked very well but I expect there's probably a 2-3x factor of optimization possible by making the system offer easier mechanisms for having the agents not duplicate work.

Can someone elaborate or point me to the next level of detail on what novelties and/or role Prove2Me is playing when autoformalizing some very large piece of mathematics?

I think of Prove2Me's role as the database the agents were using to store their progress and collaborate with. I'm sure that harnesses have some impact on token efficiency, caching, etc.

But my belief is that you'd be able to formalize FLT with a wide range of harnesses with the methods described in the post. Ultimately, once you've turned the enormity of the task into many small problems, some of which are "break X into more bite-size problems", and you have a database (Prove2Me) for keeping track of the work and searching for already-completed formalizations that you can reuse rather than duplicating, the problem is naturally parallelizable.

prove2me can ostensibly be used to formalize existing math as well as new math. The only way we distinguish right now is by labeling a mission as “open problem”. Of course, we should be a lot more invested in proof digestion and explainability if open problems get formalized before they are understood by humans. Are there good tools at “deformalization”, aka converting Lean into written math that is enlightening and enjoyable to read?

Here's a potential issue I can see with Prove2Me's mission work-flow (which tends to direct contributors' attention towards open leaf nodes): one can effectively "poison" a mission by submitting reductions showing that one of the current leaf nodes in the mission graph follows from some other statement that's actually false, or true-but-very-hard.

For example, I could submit a "proof sketch" showing that some current frontier node "X" follows from "X and the Riemann hypothesis", or even "X and the negation of FLT". Then X would then drop off the list of frontier nodes and gets replaced by the (presumably) vastly harder "X + RH". Then agents (or their human controllers) would gravitate into trying to prove "X + RH", and are likely to overlook that just proving X would suffice for the mission's end goal.

(The examples I give above are easily recognisable as either silly or malicious; but even assuming good faith by all contributors this "poisoning" issue might still arise in a different form. E.g. suppose the standard textbook proof of the mission goal goes via some well-known but hard theorem, but the mission captain wants to pursue some other, less standard strategy that avoids the standard-but-hard result. Then one can imagine well-meaning contributors dragging the mission back towards the "textbook" strategy, with reduction steps that propose as an intermediate goal the standard-but-hard result that the mission designer wanted to avoid.)

One possibility would be to give mission captains the authority to reject / deprecate reduction steps, but that seems a bit draconian, and also goes a bit against the Prove2Me ethos.

Does anyone have experience with upstreaming proofs from Prove2Me to mathlib? I'm wondering how this is supposed to work.

Suppose I carve off some small bits from the successful Prove2Me mission and submit them them as mathlib PR's. Is there a way to "rebase" the downstream Prove2Me proof once the mathlib PR's are in, replacing the carved-off bits in Prove2Me with applications of the newly-upstreamed material in mathlib? Or would it be simpler to dump the entire proof out of Prove2Me into some other repo, and then upstream stuff from there?
@Kunal Marwaha Would there be any chance of getting CSLib and Physlib added to prove2me, as allowed dependencies?

Another feature request: it would be handy if, once a mission is complete, there were an API hook for downloading a complete self-contained (modulo mathlib) proof of the mission goal, including all dependencies, for local verification / inspection / upstreaming elsewhere. As far as I can see the API only allows fetching proofs of single theorems at a time, and for large missions this gets very slow.

@junji hashimoto I’m not sure we have a good way to support that workflow. But if you want to take a graph of theorem statements in a mission and convert to natural language, you could do that within prove2me in the discussion zone. Then you could add more nodes and edges to the graph based on this. We can also consider adding tools to support this iterative improvement of proof explainability.

@David Loeffler if you merge to Mathlib, then when prove2me updates its Mathlib version, you could create the same mission statement on that new version with a simpler graph. But this will be slow process, makes more sense to take a prove2me output and put it slowly into Mathlib or maybe tau Ceti. Hope that helps.

Kunal Marwaha said:

David Loeffler if you merge to Mathlib, then when prove2me updates its Mathlib version, you could create the same mission statement on that new version with a simpler graph. But this will be slow process, makes more sense to take a prove2me output and put it slowly into Mathlib or maybe tau Ceti. Hope that helps.

The issue here is that upstreaming to mathlib would involve a lot of very small slices (new code PR's for mathlib are limited to 500 lines max); and it's extremely rare for mathlib PR's to get merged without changes – changes for the better, but changes nonetheless. So after each chunk gets merged, the rest of the downstream project repo has to be adjusted slightly to work with the final, reviewed Mathlib version of the upstreamed chunk, rather than its original draft.

It sounds like Prove2Me isn't set up for this iterative model, which is fine – that isn't its goal; but then it becomes necessary to dump the whole of the Prove2Me proof into some other repo which does support this kind of iterative upstreaming. Hence my other question.

I think the direction we can explore is pushing prove2me proofs to Tau Ceti, or some other repository that is open to large automated changes. From there we can continue to digest the proofs and go from Tau Ceti to Mathlib. Open to ideas here

Exporting to Tau Ceti makes sense (& is actually what I was planning to do with the MTT project anyway); but why not leave the decision in the hands of the user? If users can download the whole proof as a self-contained Lean project filetree (with the appropriate mathlib version as a dependency), then they are free to upload it to wherever they like, be it Tau Ceti or lean-eval or github or whatever.
Export is our most requested feature! We are figuring out the best way we can do this.

In 2011 P. Mihailescu announced a proof of the Leopoldt conjecture for CM fields (and p odd). Mihailescu had previously proved Catalan's conjecture (correctly), but the mathematical community was never convinced of his proof of Leopoldt, and the paper is on ArXiv https://arxiv.org/abs/1105.4544 but remains unpublished. We've been working on stating Leopoldt's conjecture at the formal conjectures workshop and I am optimistic that the statement formalised by AI in https://prove2.me/my-missions/fff5341b-4cd6-4a16-b2d1-957ef1193dde is an accurate formalization of the conjecture (I don't know if this link is public, it's currently in "Moderator review").

I assume that the paper will not check out, because it would be a big deal if Leopoldt was proved for CM fields. But one never knows -- Hales showed that Jordan's proof of the Jordan Curve theorem was fine even though it was commonly accepted that it was not, and the community was sceptical about the consistency of New Foundations but this was also formalized in Lean. However this might be a step too far. I am wondering what a possible failure will look like.
Non-private link to Kevin's Leopoldt project : https://prove2.me/theorems/2dd40267-fa5b-4b77-961a-e68942a6103f

I think @Kevin Buzzard you share an important sentiment. I am really trying not to diminish and hopefully to improve human understanding.

We tried to choose two campaigns carefully:

  1. The weak goldbach conjecture (for all n > 0, at most 3 primes always sum to 2n+1) as I understand is not fully accepted, although it seems Helfgott has a lot of exposition on the topic by now. A Lean proof would remove such doubt. I felt that “for all n > 0, at most 5 primes always sum to 2n+1” was a good starting point on the way to the conjecture, which I think @Tim Abbott proposed earlier on the site.
  2. The recent works improving the upper bound of omega are clever applications of the laser method, sometimes by finding particular certificates as good approximate solutions to 50+-variable problems. The most recent work used AlphaEvolve to improve a certificate. I found these incremental improvements to be difficult to certify, and so a Lean proof may help someone like me believe the output.

I think I may be slightly more optimistic about the use of slop formalization. If the theorem statement and definitions are agreed upon by humans, a slop formalization can get us a certificate of correctness. From there, we can build and experiment with “deformalization” tools that turn such slop certificates into simpler and more intuitive proofs meant for humans. In the possibility that artificial systems become superhuman at solving some math problems, I want to take advantage of those systems in a way that is harnessed for human understanding.

Concretely, improving the state of the art upper bound on omega with a slop formalization, coupled with tools to help us digest the new proof, could push us to understand the limits of the laser method and CW tensor. I imagine there are some other problems where this could be useful.

I want to tread carefully here, and hear advice from all of you.

The Weak Goldbach conjecture has two completely independent components -- the proof for n≤1030n\leq 10^{30}n≤1030 or so (by brute force computation) and the proof for n>1030n>10^{30}n>1030 (done by Helfgott's careful analysis). I would definitely recommend not using any CPU cycles on the brute force computation! This needs bespoke tools. In fact the canonical thing to do is probably formalize Helfgott's work, and then ask the AI to make it better, and see how small you can get the bound which needs to be checked by brute force :-) And then think independently about how one might formalize this. If you want to make a head start on this computation, then one of the key inputs is a verification of binary Goldbach for n<1024n<10^{24}n<1024 or so, which is where one will have to start.

Prove2Me is nice software, thank you for making it available! I tried it on one theorem from a classic paper, and have a bit of feedback. (Disclaimer: My understanding of the platform is mediated by interactions with an agent - I am grateful for corrections.)

Kunal Marwaha said:

I’m reluctant to remove all human verification but I think there could be a way to make the process lighter. If we don’t understand the target theorem statements, what is the point of autoformalizing them?

I feel like the current flow does not entirely match what tends to happen during formalization, namely that definitions and statements get revised repeatedly as various edge cases are discovered. It's not necessarily that the initial formulation is wrong—though it might be—but rather that it's not the best one to build on. It would be nice if Prove2Me made revision a first-class operation/concept, and didn't assume that the initial plan was correct, or that it was human-reviewed in entirety.

In Prove2Me, upon proposing a plan, one is asked to review all the included definitions/statements for accuracy. While I mostly agree that reviewing the target statement and its cone of dependencies is desirable, in my experiment there were also many intermediate lemmas. I felt like reviewing these would be a waste of time, so I clicked the scary "I confirm all the items are faithful to the source" button despite having 0% confidence in it. And indeed, the agent discovered an edge case later that meant one of the definitions was "bad" and should be replaced by a "better" one. The agent worked around the plan's immutability (specifically, it seems that theorem/definition descriptions are editable but formal statements are not) by introducing a new definition and editing the old one's description to say "use the other one".

Yeah, I think that's a good thought. I think the right model is one where there's human review on the main goal, and then human review before publication on what your agents proved, but I think having to spend human attention reviewing what the work is before the agents work is probably backwards with the current agents.

Thanks for the suggestion! I think if the definitions are likely to change, I would not include this in the set of "milestones". Ideally, the only Lean statetments to review when launching a mission are statements that will be proven during the mission. I am also partial to immutability of theorems and "proof sketches" because it avoids a whole category of bugs.

That being said, the mission "captain" should be able to edit the set of milestones, so that if there was an edge case, you could remove the disproved statement as a milestone and submit a corrected version of the statement, and elevate it to "milestone". How does that sound?
